newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan upbeat but concerned on stocks,inflation.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan upbeat but concerned on stocks,inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday delivered an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy but voiced concerns about skyrocketing stock prices and the risk of higher inflation.
"Even I must admit that our economic prospects in general are quite favorable," the central bank chief said in his semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins economic testimony to Congress.

"The Federal Reserve must not acquiesce in an upcreep in inflation, for acceding to higher inflation would countenance an insiduous weakening of our chances for sustaining long-run economic growth," Greenspan said.
He said he could not rule out the Fed raising rates even before higher inflation becomes evident because of the lags in which monetary policy affects the economy.
"We cannot rule out a situation in which a pre-emptive policy tightening may become appropriate," Greenspan said.
Greenspan, though, signalled that any Fed move to raise rates would not be as aggressive as in 1994/95 when the central bank doubled the federal funds rate from three to six percent.
Conditions now are different, and in fact the real, inflation-adjusted level of the funds rate coupled with the recent rise of the dollar may be enough to contain inflation, he said.
"Nonetheless," he added, "we cannot be sure. And the risks of being wrong are clearly tilted to the upside."
Fed policymakers see inflation remaining low this year, with consumer prices rising by 2.75 to 3.0 percent.

But Greenspan said that many of the factors that have held down inflation, including subdued wage demands due to worker insecurity and the dampening impact of the dollar's past rise on import prices, were temporary.

He saw the possibility of a rise this year in the so-called core inflation rate, which strips out volatile food and energy costs. A combination of higher minimum wage, increased growth of worker benefits and a continued tight labor market could put upward pressure on core inflation.
"Moreover, the effects of the sharp rise in the dollar over the last 18 months in pushing down import prices are likely to ebb over coming quarters," Greenspan said.
He said Fed policymakers see the economy growing "appreciably" this year by two to 2.5 percent. The economy grew by 3.4 percent last year on a fourth quarter-on-fourth quarter basis.
Central bank officials expect unemployment to stay roughly steady, averaging 5.25 to 5.5 percent in the fourth quarter of this year. In January, unemployment was 5.4 percent.
Greenspan spent much of his testimony discussing what he called the extraordinary rise of the stock market in recent years.
Just as he did in December when he rocked global stock prices, Greenspan again raised the question of whether so-called "irrational exuberance" is infecting the markets.
"There are reasons in the current environment to keep this question on the table," he said.
While it is possible that economic conditions have fundamentally changed for the better, Greenspan counseled caution about drawing such a conclusion.
"Participants in financial markets seem to believe that in the current benign environment the FOMC (the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee) will succeed indefinitely," Greenspan said.
"There is no evidence, however," he added, "that the business cycle has been repealed. Another recession will doubtless occur some day."

Greenspan highlighted what he called narrow yield spreads in financial markets, especially in the junk bond market, and suggested that they may be reflecting an unrealistic assessment of future risks.

Greenspan said that the central bank does not have a "firm view" that stock prices are too high or risk spreads too low. But the Fed has to be sensitive to indications of even slowly building imbalances, whatever their source, he said.

"The FOMC continues to see the distribution of inflation risks skewed to the upside and must remain especially alert to the possible emergence of imbalances in financial and product markets that ultimately could endanger the maintenance of the low inflation environment," Greenspan said.
"Sustainable economic expansion for 1997 and beyond depends on it," he added.
The FOMC left its targets for money supply growth in 1997 unchanged at 1.0 to 5.0 percent for M2, 2.0 to 6.0 percent for M3, and 3.0 to 7.0 percent for debt.
Greenspan said the FOMC remained hesitant, however, about upgrading the role of money supply measures in determining interest rates because of concern about their possible "aberrant behavior."
